newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: INTERVIEW-Paraguay bank chief says liquidity sound.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Paraguay bank chief says liquidity sound.

text.p: Paraguay's central bank chief, fresh from taking control of three troubled financial institutions, said in an interview there are no other banks that need similar state intervention.
Central Bank President Hermes Gomez Ginard told Reuters Wednesday that liquidity at the remaining 33 banks and 52 savings and loans was satisfactory.
"There are none with problems of liquidity," he said, adding "for now there is no reason" to take control of other institutions.

He defended the authorities against criticisms that they acted too slowly and should have stepped in sooner to take over Banco Union, the country's largest privately-owned bank, Ahorros Paraguayos, a savings and loan institution linked to Union, and Banco de Inversiones.
Rather, Gomez Ginard said, officials chose to let Banco Union executives come up with a restructuring plan to try to save themselves first. "We went the positive route."
However, on June 16, the central bank took over all three institutions amid allegations executives siphoned off some of the funds the state loaned them under the restructuring plan.

A judge on Thursday charged four Banco Union executives with "conspiracy to commit a crime." One of them, Francisco Scavone, is the brother of Ubaldo Scavone, who resigned as industry and trade minister on Monday for "ethical reasons."
The Scavone family is the largest shareholder in the bank.
Criminal Judge Jorge Bogarin also froze the bank accounts of the four and prohibited them from leaving the country.
Interior Minister Atilio Fernandez replaced Ubaldo Scavone Thursday. Presidential Chief of Staff Miguel Ramrez will take over Fernandez's old job.
Banco Union shareholders are scheduled to meet Friday to decide whether to inject fresh capital or to put the institution on the auction block.
Union has $190 million in deposits, and is the largest institution holding private corporate deposits and the third largest holder of public deposits.
The central bank is committed to guaranteeing deposits of up to $2,300. As such only seven percent of deposit holders can get all of their money back immediately.
An International Monetary Fund team now in Asuncion as part of a yearly visit is studying improvements to the banking system with Paraguayan authorities.
However, Gomez Ginard said the government would not ask the lending agency for financial aid.

The central bank chief acknowledged that the frozen funds could, at least temporarily, dampen investment. But a record soybean crop should continue to ensure higher gross domestic product this year. He forecast that GDP, after growing 1.3 percent last year, would rise three percent in 1997. This is down from an earlier forecast of four percent.

Gomez Ginard also predicted that inflation would be similar to last year's 8.0 percent, that the public external debt would remain around $1.3 billion and that foreign reserves would hold steady at nearly $1 billion. ((--541 318-0618))
